food.text: Egyptian cuisine leans heavily on poultry, legumes, vegetables and fruit from the rich Nile Valley and Delta. Signature dishes include ful medames, made from mashed fava beans, and koshary, made from lentils and pasta. A large share of the cuisine is vegetarian, largely because of the country's agricultural landscape.

Falafel is a deep-fried fritter of Egyptian origin. In Egypt it is most often made with fava beans, while in the Levant it is typically made with chickpeas or a blend of both. It is a popular street food throughout the Middle East.

Egyptian cuisine shaped Sudanese cooking, and the two countries share dishes such as ful medames, molokhia, umm ali and basbousa. Falafel, called tamiya in Sudan, is made with chickpeas there rather than the fava beans used in Egypt.

Nubian cooking, developed in villages around Aswan in southern Egypt, mainly uses locally grown barley, sorghum and wheat. A common bread, kabed, is made by mixing corn flour with water and baking it until crispy at the edges yet soft inside. Nubians typically eat it with milk, honey, vegetables or meat.

Nazira Nicola (1902–1992), known as Abla Nazira, trained in England and helped democratize recipes through domestic science. Her cookbook Kitab Abla Nazira, first published in 1941 as a domestic science manual, became a household staple. Through her books and radio appearances she became a national icon who promoted cooking as an essential skill for modern women.

Falafel began spreading outside Egypt after World War 1, helped by the port city of Alexandria, which allowed the dish and its name to be exported. By 1933 a falafel shop had opened in Beirut, and the dish moved down the Red Sea coast to Yemen, west into Libya and north into Turkey.

Macarona bil-bechamel is an Egyptian pasta bake of penne, spiced meat sauce and creamy béchamel. It likely reflects Greek pastitsio, an influence from the early 20th century, when a significant Greek community lived in Egypt. Greek-owned restaurants in Cairo and Alexandria helped popularize such dishes.

Cookbooks such as Kitab Abla Nazira helped cement macarona bil-bechamel in Egyptian home cooking, standardizing the dish and making it a household staple. The dish is described as a fusion of Mediterranean culinary traditions rather than a direct European import.

In the town of Mersa Matruoh, falafel was adapted by replacing fava beans with hyacinth beans and beef. In the Levant, fava beans were replaced with chickpeas. Generally, though, falafel remained unchanged as it spread.

Historically, Sudan was one of the few predominantly Muslim countries that allowed traditional and Western alcoholic drinks. Men drank millet wine, sharbot (an alcoholic drink from fermented dates), and araqi, and in the 20th century some Sudanese, influenced by Europeans, began drinking whiskey and beer. In September 1983, President Gaafar Nimeiry enacted sharia and marked the occasion by dumping alcohol into the Nile river. Since then alcohol has been banned in Sudan, and the penalty for breaking the ban is being lashed 40 times.

art.text: Between 1960 and 1980, a UNESCO-led coalition of fifty countries relocated 22 monuments in Lower Nubia to make way for the Aswan Dam. The effort led to the World Heritage Convention in 1972.
art.source_title: International Campaign to Save the Monuments of Nubia

art.text: Neo-Mamluk architecture combined modern European architecture with stylistic elements of historic Mamluk buildings in Egypt. It was mainly prominent between 1870 and 1930, and was used for government buildings, mosques and residences. It was partly an indirect expression of the beginnings of modern Egyptian nationalism.

The Museum of Modern Egyptian Art in Cairo holds more than 13,000 paintings and sculptures. They show the development of the Egyptian art movement from early 20th century pioneers to contemporary artists. The collections include work by Mahmoud Said, Ragheb Ayad, Gazbeya Sirry and Abdel Hadi Al-Gazzar.

The Abu Simbel temples were salvaged between 1964 and 1968 at a cost of about US$40 million. The whole site was cut into blocks of up to 30 tons, dismantled, and reassembled 65 metres higher and 200 metres back from the river. It was described as one of the greatest challenges of archaeological engineering in history.
art.source_title: International Campaign to Save the Monuments of Nubia

art.text: The Temple of Debod, an ancient Nubian temple, now stands in Madrid, Spain. Egypt donated it to Spain in 1968 in gratitude for Spanish help in the campaign to save Nubia's monuments. It was taken apart and rebuilt in a Madrid park between 1970 and 1972, making it one of the few works of ancient Egyptian architecture outside Egypt.

In 1952, architect Ramses Wissa Wassef founded the Ramses Wissa Wassef Art Center in Giza. He asked 14 children, mostly Copts, to develop a new artform by reviving the ancient Coptic weaving method. The weaver Maryam Hermina, born in 1932, taught them the technique.

Wael Shawky was born in 1971 in Alexandria and studied at the University of Alexandria and the University of Pennsylvania. He took part in the Venice Biennale of 2003. His provocative work explores what constitutes "normality" and "abnormality", and includes The Cave (2006) and Al Aqsa Park (2006).
Mohammed Wardi, born in 1932 near Wadi Halfa, was a Nubian Sudanese singer, poet and songwriter. He became a cultural icon of modern Sudan and sang in both Arabic and Nubian languages.

Many Nubian temples had been converted to churches in the 6th century, and many still held remnants of Christian paintings when they were relocated. In the process of dismantling the temples into blocks, the remaining Christian wall paintings were destroyed, revealing the ancient Egyptian art beneath.
art.source_title: International Campaign to Save the Monuments of Nubia

art.text: When the Temple of Debod was reassembled in Madrid, its gateways were placed in a different order than when originally erected. The gateway topped by a serpent-flanked sun was not the closest gateway to the temple proper at its original site. In February 2020, Madrid's city council unanimously decided to accelerate plans to cover the monument, after Egyptologists criticised its exposure to the elements.

Abu al-Abbas al-Mursi Mosque in Alexandria was built between 1929 and 1945 by Italian architects Eugenio Valziana and Mario Rossi. Its exterior is designed in a Neo-Mamluk style, with inspiration from the late Mamluk period in particular.
Mohammed Wardi's songs addressed romance, Nubian folklore, heritage, revolution and patriotism. Some of his political songs resulted in his being jailed.

The Egyptian Antiquities Organization rescued many smaller Nubian temples using its own resources. Work began in 1960 on Taffeh, Debod and Qertassi, followed by Dakka and Maharraqa in 1961 and Dendur in 1962. The temples of Wadi es-Sebua and Beit el Wali were moved in 1964 with a US grant.
art.source_title: International Campaign to Save the Monuments of Nubia

art.text: After Omdurman Radio chose Mohammed Wardi to sing on national broadcast in 1957, he worked together with the poet Ismail Hassan. Their collaboration resulted in more than 23 songs.

war.text: Egypt was a major battlefield in the North African campaign of the Second World War, and it was the location of the First and Second Battles of El Alamein. Even so, Egypt remained formally neutral for most of the war and only declared war on the Axis powers in the spring of 1945.

The Egyptian–Libyan War, also called the Four Day War, was a short border war fought from 21 to 24 July 1977. On 21 July a Libyan tank battalion raided the Egyptian town of Sallum, where it was ambushed and hit by a counter-attack that inflicted 50 percent casualties on the 9th Tank Battalion before it retreated. Over the whole war the Libyans lost about 400 casualties and the Egyptians at most 100, and three Soviet technicians helping the Libyans were killed in airstrikes.

In 1956 Britain, France and Israel invaded Egypt. Israel attacked on 29 October, and the United Kingdom and France joined on 31 October, seeking to depose President Gamal Abdel Nasser and regain the Suez Canal he had nationalised earlier that year. Anglo-French bombing killed hundreds of Egyptian civilians, and at Port Said the heavy street fighting and fires destroyed much of the city, killing many civilians. Estimates of Egyptian dead run from 1,000–3,000 from the Israeli invasion plus about 650 from the Anglo-French operation, against 172 Israeli dead, before pressure from the United States, the Soviet Union and the United Nations forced the withdrawal.

Since independence in 1956, Sudan has suffered repeated wars: the First Sudanese Civil War (1955–1972), the Second Sudanese Civil War (1983–2005), and the War in Darfur (2003–2020). In the early period of the first war, hundreds of northern bureaucrats, teachers and other officials serving in the south were massacred. The second war displaced more than 4 million southerners, who could not grow food or earn money, so malnutrition and starvation became widespread; it culminated in the secession of South Sudan on 9 July 2011. In Darfur, Arab militias (Janjaweed) allied with the government were accused of atrocities and, according to the rebels, ethnic cleansing, and estimates of the dead range from under twenty thousand to several hundred thousand, from combat or from starvation and disease. A new civil war began in 2023.

Under the 1936 Anglo-Egyptian Treaty, British troops in Egypt were limited to the Suez Canal until 1956 and Alexandria until 1944, except in wartime, when Britain could increase its troop count. Egypt had to assist Britain materially in a war but was not obligated to fight, so it could stay technically neutral.

Relations between the two states worsened after Egyptian President Anwar Sadat rebuffed Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi's entreaties to unify their countries. Sadat also began pursuing peace negotiations with Israel after the Yom Kippur War in 1973, and Libya then began sponsoring dissidents and assassination plots to undermine him. Egypt responded in kind, supporting subversion in Libya, possibly including encouragement of plots to assassinate Gaddafi. By early 1976 Libyan troops on the border were clashing with Egyptian border guards, and on 19 July 1977 the Egyptian government reported that nine of its soldiers were killed in a drawn-out firefight.

Israel's four-month occupation of the Gaza Strip and the Sinai Peninsula won it freedom of navigation through the Straits of Tiran. The UN estimated that 447 to 550 Palestinian civilians were killed by Israeli troops in the first weeks of the occupation of Gaza, and how they died is disputed: Israel says street-fighting, while Palestinians said unarmed civilians were executed at Khan Yunis. After taking Rafah, Israeli troops killed 111 people, including 103 refugees, in its refugee camp. The Suez Canal, meanwhile, was closed from October 1956 to March 1957.

On 4 February 1942, after the British ambassador Sir Miles Lampson had threatened King Farouk, he arrived at Abdeen Palace with British soldiers and tanks. He threatened to bombard the palace and to force the king's abdication and exile unless he gave in. Lampson ordered Farouk to sign an abdication statement, and Farouk offered to call Nahhas to form a cabinet. The Abdeen Palace Incident humiliated the king and Egypt, showed that neither the king nor the Wafd could challenge British influence, and its results contributed directly to the Egyptian revolution of 1952.

Sadat moved two mechanised divisions, totaling 25,000 to 35,000 troops, to the border and transferred 80 combat aircraft to Marsa Matruh Airbase, Egypt's westernmost airfield. Alarmed, Gaddafi sent an additional 3,000 to 5,000 troops and 150 tanks to the border.

France was allied with Israel against Egypt, partly because Egypt supported the Algerian National Liberation Front rebels. In 1956 Israeli defense official Shimon Peres told the French that Israel had decided on war with Egypt, wanting to fight before Egypt received even more Soviet weapons.

After the 1956 war, Egyptian Interior Minister Zakaria Mohieddin said that 12,000 of Egypt's 18,000 British and French citizens were ordered to be expelled, and that their properties were seized by the Egyptian government. Egyptian soldiers were sent to British and French properties, carried out search operations, and ordered the owners to leave within a week. The owners had to hand their property over to the Egyptian government. The article describes these measures as retaliation for the British, French and Israeli invasion of Egypt.
war.source_title: 20th century departures of foreign nationals from Egypt

war.text: After ambushing the Libyan raiders at Sallum, Egyptian forces launched a large counter-attack. They bombed Gamal Abdel Nasser Airbase from the air and sent a mechanised force 24 kilometres into Libyan territory before withdrawing. The Libyans lost a total of 60 tanks and armoured personnel carriers in the fighting. Egyptian jets also made low passes over Libyan villages without opening fire, which reportedly sent thousands of civilians fleeing towards Benghazi.

literature.text: A former head of the General Egyptian Book Organization said Egypt's cultural production sees roughly 18,000 new titles annually. Around 10,000 of these are original works by Egyptian authors.

Naguib Mahfouz won the 1988 Nobel Prize in Literature. By 1999 he was one of only three Egyptians to have received a Nobel Prize, alongside Anwar Sadat (Peace, 1978) and Ahmed Zewail (Chemistry, 1999).

The 1990s brought a new literary movement to Egypt, born of socio-economic, cultural and political crises facing the young. Its writers produced irrational and fragmented works about isolated individuals coping with an ever-expanding and changing Arab culture.
Edwar al-Kharrat embodied Egypt's 60s Generation of writers. He founded Galerie 68, an Arabic literary magazine that gave a voice to the avant-garde writers of the time.

New and entrepreneurial publishers such as Dar Sharqiyat and Dar Merit made it easier for new authors to be published in the 1990s. The resulting surge brought experimentation with traditional themes, a greater emphasis on the personal, an absence of major political concerns, and a more refined use of language.

Husni Sulayman founded Dar Sharqiyat, a small-scale publishing house that printed avant-garde work during the 1990s. Financial difficulties led to its replacement by Dar Merit as a leading avant-garde publisher.

Egypt's population nearly doubled after 1980, reaching 81 million in 2008. The rural-urban migration this caused gave rise to the Arabic term al-madun al-'ashwa'iyyah, or "haphazard city," around Cairo. Unemployment remained high and living expenses rose amid the overcrowding, and the difficulties of living in poverty inspired a new Egyptian literature focused on crises.

Because Dar Sharqiyat printed so much of the new writing, many critics came to call the new generation of Egyptian writers the Sharqiyyat generation. The label ties a whole literary wave to one small publishing house.

science.text: Egyptian chemist Ahmed Zewail won the 1999 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for his work on femtochemistry. He was born in 1946 in Damanhur, south-east of Alexandria, and became one of only a few Egyptians to win a Nobel Prize.

Modern scientists use radiocarbon dating to help date Ancient Egypt. It is especially useful for the Early Dynastic period, where scholars have only been able to agree within a range of about three or four centuries. The results are roughly consistent with Shaw's conventional chronology.

Ahmed Zewail won the 1999 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for his work on femtochemistry, becoming the third Egyptian Nobel laureate after Anwar Sadat (Peace, 1978) and Naguib Mahfouz (Literature, 1988). That year he also received Egypt's highest state honor, the Grand Collar of the Nile.

Ahmed Zewail was raised in Disuq and moved to the United States to complete his PhD at the University of Pennsylvania. In 1976 he was awarded a faculty appointment at Caltech, where he has remained since.
A 2013 radiocarbon study found that the First Dynasty began in the 32nd or 31st century. That is compatible with scholarly opinions placing it between the 34th and 30th centuries.

The radiocarbon date for the Thera eruption, between 1627 and 1600 BC, is off by a full century from the c. 1500 BC date traditionally accepted in archaeology. Since 2012 some have suggested a compromise date in the mid 16th century BC, but as of 2023 the problem was still unresolved.

Alternative chronologies challenged the scholarly consensus. The Glasgow Chronology, proposed 1978 to 1982, lowers New Kingdom dates by as much as 500 years. The New Chronology of the 1990s lowers them by as much as 350 years.
In the same year as his Nobel Prize, Ahmed Zewail received Egypt's highest state honor, the Grand Collar of the Nile. The award recognized a scientist whose career had been built largely abroad.

The Centuries of Darkness model of 1991, by Peter James and colleagues, would move the end of the Egyptian New Kingdom from 1070 BC to around 825 BC. It argued that miscalculations of the Third Intermediate Period required lowering all earlier dates too.

politics.text: Egypt was occupied by British forces in 1882, and the occupation lasted exactly 40 years until a unilateral declaration in February 1922. Despite four reservations, it made Egypt the first Arab country to gain official recognition of its independence from European colonialism. The last British troops did not leave until 18 June 1956.
politics.source_title: History of Egypt under the British

politics.text: The Muhammad Ali dynasty ruled Egypt for a century and a half until the Egyptian Revolution of 1952. King Farouk was forced to abdicate in favor of his infant son Fuad II, and administration passed to the Free Officers Movement under Mohamed Naguib and Gamal Abdel Nasser. On 18 June 1953 the revolutionaries abolished the monarchy and declared Egypt a republic.

In March and April 1919, mass demonstrations in Egypt became uprisings, known in Egypt as the 1919 Revolution. Anticolonial riots and British suppression of them led to the death of some 800 people. Almost daily unrest continued through the rest of the spring.
politics.source_title: History of Egypt under the British

politics.text: Abbas II, the last Khedive of Egypt and the Sudan, was deposed by the British on 18 December 1914 after they declared Egypt a Sultanate under their protection. They believed he was plotting against their rule and had appealed to Egyptians and Sudanese to support the Central Powers. His deposition marked the de jure end of nearly four centuries of Ottoman Egypt.

Farouk's reign was marked by nationalist discontent over the continuing British occupation, royal corruption and incompetence, and the disastrous Palestine War of 1948 to 1949. These factors terminally undermined his position and paved the way for the 1952 revolution.

Britain proclaimed Sudan an Anglo-Egyptian Condominium rather than an integral part of Egypt, which Egyptians continually rejected. They insisted on the 'unity of the Nile Valley'. Fuad and his son Farouk stressed the title 'King of Egypt and Sudan', and the dispute lasted until Sudan's independence in 1956.

Although Muslims and Christians share a national identity in Egypt, sectarian violence has periodically erupted. Major incidents include the 2000–2001 Kosheh massacres, which resulted in 21 deaths, attacks on churches in 2006, the 2010 Nag Hammadi massacre, and the 2011 Alexandria bombing, which killed 21 people.

To the surprise of the British authorities, Egyptian women also demonstrated in 1919, led by Huda Sha'rawi. The first women's demonstration was held on Sunday, 16 March 1919, followed by another on Thursday, 20 March. Sha'rawi would become the leading feminist voice in Egypt in the first half of the twentieth century.
politics.source_title: History of Egypt under the British

politics.text: Muhammad Naguib, who helped lead the 1952 revolution, was half-Sudanese and had been born and raised in Khartoum. The new government under him and Gamal Abdel Nasser made Sudanese independence a priority. Britain conceded in 1953, and Sudan became independent on 1 January 1956.

During World War II, Egypt hosted thousands of British troops as its treaty required, yet it stayed formally neutral and only declared war on the Axis powers in the spring of 1945. The 1936 Anglo-Egyptian Treaty gave Britain the legal right to fight on Egyptian soil while Egypt kept the right to remain technically neutral.

Abbas II was wounded in the hands and cheeks in a failed assassination attempt in Constantinople on 25 July 1914. He formally abdicated on 12 May 1931 and retired to Switzerland, where he wrote The Anglo-Egyptian Settlement. He died in Geneva on 19 December 1944, 30 years to the day after his reign as Khedive ended.

Hussein Kamel issued restrictive orders stripping the deposed Abbas II of property in Egypt and Sudan and forbidding contributions to him. The orders barred Abbas from entering Egyptian territory and took away his right to sue in Egyptian courts. They did not, however, prevent his progeny from exercising their rights.

philosophy.text: Islam is the state religion of Egypt, and religion shapes many aspects of social life. The country is majority Sunni Muslim, estimated at 85 to 95% of the population, and the next largest group is Coptic Orthodox Christians, at an estimated 5 to 15%.

Many customs and beliefs practiced in Egypt today, such as funerary laments, rural food traditions and ideas about the afterlife, can be traced to ancient Egyptian origins. Even when new religions replaced older ones, Egyptians often reinterpreted them through inherited cultural lenses, so their civilizational identity stayed intact.

Religion has been excluded from Egypt's census since 2006, so available figures are only estimates by religious and non-governmental agencies. Christians allege that they have been systemically under-counted in existing censuses, and the exact numbers remain controversial.

State-sanctioned persecution of Egypt's Baháʼís began after the monarchy was dissolved in 1953. It culminated in Law 263 in 1960, which banned all Baháʼí institutions and community activities in the country. Because their faith was not recognized, Baháʼís could not record it on national identity cards, and without valid cards they struggled to register their children in school, open bank accounts, or start businesses. Tensions remained high during the 2011 Egyptian revolution, including homes being burnt.

The 2021–2022 Arab Barometer survey reported a resurgence in religious identification in Egypt. 95% of Egyptians described themselves as religious or somewhat religious, a 6% increase from the 2018 figures.

It is difficult to count atheists in Egypt because of persecution by the religious establishments and the social stigma of identifying publicly as non-religious. The 2020 US report on international religious freedom says there are no reliable estimates. People who criticise Islam or Christianity can be tried under the blasphemy law, and outspoken atheists such as Alber Saber and Kareem Amer have been convicted under it. A study citing the 2018 Arab Barometer Wave V survey found that around 11% of Egyptians identified as not religious, and about 20% of young Egyptians did.

Kemetism is a neopagan revival of the ancient Egyptian religion that emerged during the 1970s. Its followers do not consider themselves direct descendants of the ancient religion and speak instead of its recreation or restoration.

According to reports in 2006, Egyptian Baháʼís had difficulty obtaining documents from government authorities. Because police regularly detained people without correct documents, some Baháʼís stayed at home to avoid arrest.

culture.text: Football is the most popular sport in Egypt, and its clubs Zamalek and Al Ahly are known throughout Africa. The national team has won the African Cup of Nations a record 7 times, in 1957, 1959, 1986, 1998, 2006, 2008 and 2010. Egypt was also the first African country to join FIFA.

Egyptian cinema has flourished since the 1930s, and the capital has been dubbed the "Hollywood of the Middle East". Cairo hosts the Cairo International Film Festival every year. The International Federation of Film Producers Associations rated it among the 11 top-class film festivals worldwide.

Since the end of World War I, some of the Middle East's biggest musical stars have been Egyptian. Modern Egyptian music became a core of Middle Eastern music thanks to the popularity of Egyptian cinema and music industries and Egypt's political influence on its neighbors.

The 20th century's most important Egyptian composers and singers include Sayed Darwish, Umm Kulthum, Mohammed Abdel Wahab, Abdel Halim Hafez and Baligh Hamdy. Some, like Abd el-Halim Hafez, were associated with the Egyptian nationalist movement from 1952 onward.

In 1925, Egypt became the first Muslim country to legally recognize the Baháʼí Faith as an independent religion distinct from Islam. After the 1953 dissolution of the monarchy, state-sanctioned persecution began, and Law 263 in 1960 banned all Baháʼí institutions and community activities in Egypt. Baháʼís who lacked correct documents risked detention by police, so some stayed at home to avoid arrest. During the 2011 Egyptian revolution, tensions ran high and homes were burnt.

Egypt's foreign resident population numbered around 200,000 by the end of World War 1, including British, French, Greeks, Italians, Armenians, Maltese and Jews. Known as the Mutamassirun, these communities mostly departed during the 20th century amid political instability, the Suez Crisis, the abolition of the capitulations system and the rise of Egyptian nationalism under Gamal Abdel Nasser. In 1956 Egypt's Minister of Interior Zakaria Mohieddin said that of Egypt's 18,000 British and French citizens, 12,000 were ordered to be expelled, and their properties were seized by the government.
culture.source_title: 20th century departures of foreign nationals from Egypt

culture.text: Metqal Qenawi's Les Musiciens du Nil are the most popular Sa'idi group, playing folk music from Upper Egypt. The government chose them to represent Egyptian folk music abroad, and they toured Europe for over three decades. After their 1983 performance at the World of Music and Dance Festival, they signed to Peter Gabriel's label Real World-Carolina and featured on his album Passion.

Alhour, launched in 2017, is Egypt's first all-female Muslim recitation choir. In the region, maqams (the Arabic chanting discipline) are almost always sung by men, and women who perform music or sing publicly are often viewed as promiscuous. Alhour's members are challenging these deep-rooted taboos about women singing in public or reciting from the Quran in the socially conservative country.

The Egyptian national basketball team holds the record for best performance at the Basketball World Cup and the Summer Olympics among Middle Eastern and African teams. Egypt hosted the 2017 FIBA Under-19 Basketball World Cup and is the only African country to host an official basketball world cup at junior or senior level.

Gamal Abdel Nasser's new regime reneged on his assurances to the Greeks, who had joined the Egyptian Army against British and French troops during the Suez Crisis. Between 1956 and 1960 Greeks were included in the measures targeting foreigners, and with financial assistance from the Greek government many began to leave, so that the Greek population in Egypt decreased by 80%. Many Greek schools, churches, small communities and institutions closed, though many continue to function today. The Arab-Israeli war of 1967 also uprooted the sizable Greek community in the Suez Canal cities, especially in Port Said.
culture.source_title: 20th century departures of foreign nationals from Egypt
